analysis.one_liner: Subjects FDIC-insured industrial bank owners to federal banking supervision for the first time.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill to close the industrial bank loophole died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Industrial banks take FDIC-insured deposits just like regular banks, but under a decades-old loophole their owners — commercial companies like retailers, lenders, and payment apps — are not supervised the way normal bank owners are by the Federal Reserve. This bill would give the FDIC the power to examine and restrict those parent companies, require a two-thirds vote of the FDIC board plus a public hearing to approve pending charter applications, and automatically deny any pending application not approved by September 30, 2024. It also would let regulators block a transfer of control unless the buyer is already a fully supervised banking company.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors and taxpayers who stand behind the FDIC insurance fund, and traditional banks that compete against industrial banks that answer to no consolidated federal regulator.

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDIC the same power to examine and demand reports from industrial bank parent companies that the Federal Reserve has over normal bank holding companies, with enforcement authority under the same rules the Fed uses.

Requires pending deposit insurance applications, submitted on or before September 23, 2021, to get a 90-day public comment period, a public hearing, and approval by two-thirds of the FDIC board — and deems any application not approved by September 30, 2024 denied.

Directs the FDIC to disapprove a change of control of an industrial bank unless the acquirer is itself subject to consolidated Federal Reserve supervision as a bank holding company or similar entity, closing the door on new commercial owners buying into insured deposits.
Lets regulators impose conditions or restrictions on parent companies or their non-bank subsidiaries to protect the safety of the insured bank.

analysis.who_pays: Fintech companies, large retailers, and other nonfinancial businesses that want to charter industrial banks to access insured deposits and payments without full supervision; some consumers could face less competition in lending and payments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fintechs and commercial firms seeking bank charters

drawbacks.text: Industrial banks have expanded access to loans, credit cards, and payment services, often for borrowers and businesses that traditional banks overlook; shutting off new charters could reduce competition and raise costs for some consumers, an objection the industry makes in good faith.

The bill grandfathers industrial banks approved for deposit insurance on or before September 23, 2021 from the full bank-holding-company definition, so the loophole stays open for those institutions — they only get tailored supervision rather than the treatment the bill applies to newcomers.
The September 30, 2024 deadline denies pending applications wholesale regardless of their individual merits, a blunt instrument that blocks even applications that might have been safe.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but technical: insured deposits and the taxpayer-backed insurance fund end up under the same scrutiny whether the bank is owned by a bank holding company or by a retailer or payment app. The cost is some loss of competition and credit access if fewer industrial banks can be chartered. The grandfather clause means the fix is partial rather than complete, and the blanket deadline skips case-by-case review. On balance the bill addressed a genuine safety gap with modest consumer cost, and it died without any vote or hearing on the trade-offs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2023 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on December 14, 2023, joined by five original cosponsors: Sens. Kennedy, Casey, Van Hollen, Braun, and Wicker.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill drew bipartisan sponsorship, with three of 49 Senate Republicans and two of 48 Senate Democrats cosponsoring.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fintech and commercial firms that want to own insured banks came out ahead: the loophole stayed open, existing industrial banks kept their lighter-touch treatment, and no new supervision of their parent companies ever took effect. Taxpayers and community banks gained nothing from a bill that never moved.

against.name: Fintech and payment companies seeking industrial bank charters
against.role: Nonfinancial firms that own or want to own FDIC-insured industrial banks
against.what_they_did: The fintech and payments industry publicly opposed federal supervision of industrial bank parent companies during the period when Congress considered such measures, arguing industrial banks expand access to credit and payment services.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Democrat and the five cosponsors split 3 Republicans to 2 Democrats, but the Banking Committee — chaired during most of this period by the sponsor himself — never acted on it.

industries.industry: Fintech and payment companies seeking industrial bank charters
industries.note: The bill would have blocked or delayed new insured-bank charters for nonfinancial companies, which use industrial banks to offer lending and payment services outside traditional banking rules. They argue this expands consumer access; the bill's premise is that insured deposits should not sit behind lightly supervised commercial owners.

Industrial banks compete with traditional banks while their commercial owners escape the consolidated Federal Reserve supervision banks face. Bringing those owners under FDIC supervision levels the competitive field and protects the shared deposit insurance fund.

industries.industry: Large commercial conglomerates with existing industrial banks
industries.note: The bill grandfathers industrial banks approved on or before September 23, 2021 from the bank holding company definition, but subjects their parent companies to FDIC examination and restricts who can take them over — a lighter touch than full bank-holding-company status.
